extracted.intended_audience: writers (and informed readers) of historical/creative essays and narrative non‑fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for composing readable, fair, and geographically grounded historical/creative essays — covering narrative promises to readers, contextualizing characters by climate/race/time, and clear geographical schematization. Useful for authors planning multi-part historical works with illustrative material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promise-keeping / meeting reader expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: When you promise consideration of a point in one chapter, follow through in the next; avoid a habit of promising one thing and pursuing another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author observes: 'if ever I promise, in one number or chapter, careful consideration of any particular point in the next, the next never does touch upon the promised point at all.' He resolves 'to watch, and I hope partly to correct myself in this fault of promise breaking, and at whatever sacrifice of my variously fluent or re-fluent humour, to tell in each successive chapter in some measure what the reader justifiably expects to be told.' Use this as explicit guidance to structure chapters so that promised topics are addressed and reader expectations respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartiality and largeness of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Favor impartiality and a broad perspective over narrow partisanship or hired belligerence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The writer notes that his digressive manner 'is indeed extremely conducive to impartiality and largeness of view.' Impartiality is presented as a virtue for historical/narrative treatment — aim to present multiple sides, avoid simple vilification or hagiography, and allow complexity to remain visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextualize characters by climate, race, and time
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand or depict a person, consider the climate they live in, their race (as social/cultural grouping), and the historical time that shapes them: 'In what climate is he? Of what race? At what time?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text insists 'He can only be what these conditions permit.' Use environmental, cultural, and temporal context to make characters’ behavior plausible and sympathetic; judge characters first by love, then pity, then humility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truthful mapping: accurate representation of both world and inner life
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers need 'truthful maps of the world to begin with, and truthful maps of our own hearts to end with.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is both literal (geography, boundaries) and figurative (psychology, motive). Avoid slovenly or dishonest simplifications of place or motive; strive for honesty in external description and inner characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid biased or distorted representation (beware projection/projectional tricks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let the method of depiction (e.g., map projection) distort the reader's sense of proportion or importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: Mercator's projection makes British possessions seem disproportionately large; 'the brilliant crimson with which all our landed property is coloured cannot but impress the innocent reader with the idea of a universal flush of freedom and glory.' When portraying scope or significance, choose representations that do not mislead or flatter a viewpoint by technical distortion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clear large-scale schemata (e.g., Gothic vs Classic; climatic zones) to organize narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide and classify large subjects into memorable, stable schemata (zones, opposing terms) to give readers a workable map of historical relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author proposes dividing Europe into 'four Gothic countries' and 'four Classic countries' and three north-south zones; he argues this aids comprehension: 'You have thus, easily and clearly memorable, twelve countries...you have the ground of all useful profane history mapped out in the simplest terms.' Use such schemata as organizing devices while noting their limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize geographic and natural constraints over transient political boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize mountains, seas, rivers and climate as enduring determinants of peoples and history, rather than ephemeral political lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text advises: 'you must never allow your mind to be disturbed by the accidental changes of political limit... eternal bars and doors are set to it by the mountains and seas.' In historical narrative, foreground enduring geography as causal or explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn and use meaningful names for personages
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach readers the names and the meanings of names because names can 'fateful[ly] express' character and destiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author provides a list of characters with etymologies ('Clovis... Glorious Holiness', 'Clotilde... Glorious Battle-maid'). Consider the etymology or resonance of names as an element of characterization and thematic reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing history to facile 'suppositions' or purely speculative explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist the modern habit of 'reducing all history whatever to 'the supposition that'...' — do not explain complex events by a single speculative engineering of motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A footnote warns against over-skeptical 'reductions' (e.g., alleging clerical engineers undermined walls to explain miracles). Maintain respect for complexity and for the way myths/legends function; avoid cynical one-liners that collapse rich historical phenomena into single hypothetical devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer concrete anecdote and moral ambiguity over simplistic moralizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use vivid episodes (e.g., the vase of Soissons) to open moral questions and avoid unnuanced condemnation or applause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The vase anecdote is presented with alternate morals and with reflection on the king's pause and later revenge; the author stresses that 'we never can know the truth of Sin; for its nature is to deceive alike on the one side the Sinner, on the other the Judge.' Let stories show complexity; avoid flattening them into moral slogans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust form and edition to audience and practical use (large edition, travellers' edition, subscribers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor form, size, and supplementary material (illustrations, reduced editions) to the intended readers and modes of consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author outlines plans: 'One illustration at least will be given with each chapter... a smaller edition... will commonly be printed in reduced form for travellers and non-subscribers; but otherwise... furnished to subscribers only.' Consider multiple formats and illustrative support depending on readership and purpose.
